The Speaker of the Lagos State House of Assembly, Mudashiru Obasa, has urged lawmakers across the world to translate commitments to ending hunger and malnutrition into enforceable laws, adequate budgetary allocations and effective oversight mechanisms. Obasa made the call at just-concluded Third Global Parliamentary Summit on Hunger and Malnutrition, held at the Parliament of Kenya, Nairobi. This is contained in statement signed by his Chief Press Secretary, Mr Tayo Oyeshina to newsmen on Thursday in Lagos. The two-day summit, organised by the Parliament of Kenya, the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO) and the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation (AECID),held between Nov.16 and 17. Represented by a delegation of legislators, senior assembly officials and legislative aides, Obasa presented Nigeria’s and Lagos approaches to addressing food insecurity and strengthening agrifood systems. He said the Federal Government, under President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda, had approved the National Nutrition Bill 2026 and the revised National Policy on Food and Nutrition. According to him, the initiatives will provide a framework for improved nutrition governance, sustainable funding, institutional coordination and effective implementation of food interventions nationwide. On Lagos State’s efforts, Obasa said the government had adopted a five-point strategy focusing on technology, interstate collaboration, investment in farmers, reduction of post-harvest losses and improved access to affordable and nutritious food. He explained that the strategy was informed by the state’s limited arable land and growing population of more than 22 million people. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. He said the facility, commissioned in January 2023, had an annual production capacity of 2.8 million 50kg bags of rice and was expected to generate 1,500 direct and 254,000 indirect jobs. The Speaker also highlighted the N500 billion Offtake Guarantee Fund under the ‘Produce for Lagos’ initiative, designed to address supply chain challenges and improve access to agricultural produce. He said the initiative would provide working capital for bulk traders and logistics operators, alongside credit support for food producers, to strengthen food supply and attract private investment into agriculture. Obasa added that the Lagos Fresh Food Hub had completed and commissioned mid-level food hub facilities in Mushin, Abijo in Ibeju-Lekki and Agege. He added that construction of a 500-hectare central food logistics hub in Epe had reached 70 per cent completion. According to him, the facility would incorporate cold-chain storage, dry-chain infrastructure and other facilities to improve food preservation, handling, transportation and distribution. He also said the Assembly had prioritised agriculture and food systems through its appropriation laws, with more than N80 billion allocated across recent budget cycles. “We are currently advancing the Food Hub Bill, which will formalise market operations, reduce the constraints of informal trading, improve food safety standards and strengthen coordination across the value chain,” he said. Obasa stressed that legislation, adequate funding and effective oversight were critical to achieving food security and tackling malnutrition. “As legislators, we back every effort to combat hunger and malnutrition with concrete laws and oversight. “The Lagos State House of Assembly will continue to deepen this work. We will maintain and increase budgetary allocations for resilient agrifood systems, strengthen oversight mechanisms and refine laws to promote climate-smart agriculture,” he said. He reaffirmed state’s readiness to share its experiences and collaborate with other legislatures to develop sustainable solutions to food insecurity. “Lagos stands ready to share its experiences, to learn from the innovations of other legislatures across the world, and to work in solidarity with every parliament represented here. “Together, let us legislate for a hunger-free future,” he said. In his keynote address, Kenyan President William Ruto said ending hunger required legislation, adequate budgets and effective oversight, describing these as core responsibilities of parliamentarians. Ruto warned that Africa could account for nearly 60 per cent of the world’s hungry population by 2030, if urgent action was not taken. He called for increased domestic resource mobilisation, reduced dependence on food imports, improved irrigation systems and expanded school feeding programmes. The Kenyan president also urged lawmakers to enact laws protecting food security programmes from political changes, stressing that sustained funding was essential. “A right without a budget line is a slogan,” Ruto said.
